Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I have failed in my most important role in life
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, dogs as a trigger is possible but, in the absence of any related memory content, threat theme, or appraisal linking animals to the event, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the profile and is hard to integrate clinically with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal that something about the patient made the event happen is difficult to reconcile with terrorism trauma, which is typically externally caused and indiscriminate. Self-blame can occur, but this specific intrinsic-causation item is not well supported by the rest of the profile and is clinically hard to explain here.

vignette:
Marisol is a 78-year-old widowed Salvadoran American woman who works part-time as a call center agent from her apartment in a mid-sized Texas city. She was referred for psychological evaluation following a routine check-in with her primary care physician, who noted her elevated distress and persistent somatic complaints. Her PCL-5 score of 73 places her in a range of severe posttraumatic stress, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions was one of a woman quietly carrying an enormous weight, largely alone.

Several years ago, Marisol was present during a terrorist attack at a public market she visited regularly - a place she had gone to since arriving in the United States decades earlier, a place that smelled like the markets of her childhood. The attack unfolded without warning. There was an explosion, then chaos, then a period she describes only in fragments: a ringing in her ears, the sensation of something striking the back of her neck, the sight of strangers on the ground. What she cannot account for - and what distresses her profoundly - is a stretch of time she simply cannot reconstruct. She knows she was there. She knows she survived. But there is a gap, and no amount of effort has filled it. When she tries to speak about what happened, she finds herself unable to locate the words, as though language itself has been stripped from the experience. She will start a sentence and stop, her hands moving slightly, reaching for something that isn't there. She has described this to the evaluator as feeling like she is trying to explain a colour that has no name.

In the months following the attack, Marisol quietly reorganized her life around what she could not bear to approach. She has not returned to that part of the city. The anniversary of the attack passes each year with her curtains drawn and her phone turned off. What she has come to believe, with a certainty that feels absolute to her, is that she failed the people she loved most - that a woman of her age and experience should have done something, helped someone, been more than a survivor. Her late husband, she says, would have acted. She has also come to believe that there is simply no future left for her, that the arc of her life ended at that market and what remains is a kind of aftermath. What frightens her most is not death but the suspicion that she cannot protect anyone she loves from harm - that bad things will find their way to her and to those around her, and she will be powerless each time.

This sense of helplessness has shaped how she moves through her days. She works her call center shifts from home, and it is there that her triggers arrive uninvited. Callers sometimes describe losses - a family member's illness, a bereavement, a sudden tragedy - and when they do, Marisol feels something shift in her body before she is fully aware of what she is hearing. The pain in her neck, a dull and persistent ache she has had since the attack, sharpens in those moments. She has learned to mute herself briefly on calls when this happens, to breathe, to wait for it to pass. Her supervisors have noted that her call times have lengthened and that she occasionally disconnects before resolution. She has not explained why.

She has also withdrawn from her daughter and her two grandchildren, keeping visits short and conversation light. Being emotionally close to them, she has found, opens something in her she cannot close again easily. It is safer, she has decided, to love them from a careful distance.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was not a crisis but an accumulation - a grandchild's offhand question about why she never talks about the past, and the realisation that she had no answer. She arrived at the intake quietly, dressed carefully, and said very little at first. What she hoped for, she eventually offered, was simply to find the words.
